a: in a certain place praying
p: Luke shows Jesus praying at every turning point. Here his own prayer is what makes a disciple ask to be taught.
b: More than any other Gospel, Luke pictures Jesus at prayer: at his baptism (3:21), alone in the wilderness (5:16), all night before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), on the mountain (9:28–29), on the Mount of Olives (22:41) and on the cross (23:34, 46). Here Luke does not say what Jesus prayed. The point is that watching him pray makes a disciple want to learn. The Lord's Prayer comes in Luke as an answer to a request, not, as in Matthew, as part of a sermon (Matthew 6:9–13). Acts carries the theme on: the church is born praying (Acts 1:14; 2:42).

a: the way John also taught his disciples
p: Teachers gave their followers a prayer of their own. John's prayer has not survived.
b: Luke has already said that "John's disciples often fast and say their prayers" (5:33). A group's own prayer marked it off from others, as the hymns of the Dead Sea Scrolls did for the community at Qumran. The disciple is asking for something like a badge of belonging: a short prayer that says who Jesus' followers are. No prayer of John's has come down to us. Followers of John were still around years later, as far away as Ephesus (Acts 18:25; 19:1–7).

a: When you pray
p: Luke's prayer opens with one word, "Father": probably the Aramaic Abba that Jesus used.
b: Matthew's form, used in churches, begins "Our Father, who is in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). Luke's oldest manuscripts have only Pater, "Father" (see the variant). Behind it most scholars hear the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane in Mark 14:36, which Paul says believers also cry out by the Spirit (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). Joachim Jeremias argued that such a plain address to God was unheard of in Jewish prayer. Later scholars have softened this: Jews did call God "Father" (Isaiah 63:16; Sirach 23:1), but Jesus made it the center of his own prayer and gave it to his followers.
r: Matthew 6:9; Mark 14:36; Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6; Isaiah 63:16; Sirach 23:1

a: may your name be honored as holy
p: The opening pair, God's name made holy and his kingdom come, closely matches the old Jewish prayer called the Kaddish.
b: The Kaddish, an Aramaic prayer still said in synagogues, begins: "Magnified and sanctified be his great name ... and may he establish his kingdom in your lifetime." Its exact first-century form is unknown, but the pairing is old. Jesus' prayer is a Jewish prayer in shape and content. What Luke's short form adds is its directness: two wishes for God's name and kingdom, then three requests for bread, forgiveness and protection. See the notes on Matthew 6:9–13 for the longer form.

a: Keep giving us each day
p: Matthew asks "give us today"; Luke asks God to keep giving, "each day," like the manna.
b: Luke uses a present-tense command, didou, "keep on giving," and the phrase to kath' hēmeran, "day by day," where Matthew has the one-time dos, "give," and sēmeron, "today" (Matthew 6:11). Luke's form fits a church that prays the prayer every day over many years. The picture behind both is the manna, which Israel gathered "each day's share on its own day" (Exodus 16:4). On the hard word epiousios, rendered here "for the coming day," see the note on Matthew 6:11.
orig: δίδου ... τὸ καθ' ἡμέραν (didou ... to kath' hēmeran)

a: forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who owes us
p: Luke says "sins" in the request but keeps "owes" in the next clause, a trace of the debt language in Matthew.
b: Matthew prays "forgive us the debts we owe" (Matthew 6:12). Luke, writing for Greek readers who would not take "debts" as "sins," writes hamartias, "sins," but then says we forgive "everyone who owes us" (opheilonti). In Aramaic ḥôbā, "debt," was an ordinary word for sin, so the two forms say the same thing. Luke's "for we ourselves also forgive" is in the present tense: it describes the praying community's habit, not a price paid in advance. Luke uses the same picture in 7:41–43 and 13:4.

a: at midnight
p: In a village, a guest had to be fed, and the whole village's honor was at stake.
b: Travelers often walked in the cool of the evening and arrived late. A host had to set food before a guest, even at midnight, and in a small village a failure would shame not only the host but the neighbors too. Women baked bread for several days at a time, and people knew who had some left. Three loaves is a meal for one man. Kenneth Bailey, drawing on long experience of Middle Eastern village life, argued that every hearer would answer Jesus' question "Which of you...?" with "No one would refuse!"

a: my children are in bed with me
p: A peasant family slept together on one raised platform. Unbolting the door would wake them all.
b: Most village houses in Galilee had one main room, with the family sleeping on mats on a raised part of the floor and sometimes the animals below. The door was barred with a heavy wooden bolt. Getting up, stepping over the children and drawing the bolt would wake the whole household. The excuse sounds reasonable to a modern reader, but Jesus' question expects his hearers to find it unthinkable: no friend would answer like that.

a: because of his shamelessness
p: The word means "shamelessness." It is unclear whether it describes the man knocking or the man in bed.
b: Anaideia means lack of shame, and is usually a bad quality. The KJV's "importunity" (persistence) made the parable a lesson in nagging God. But the Greek "his" is ambiguous. (1) The asker's bold, shameless knocking wins in the end; Klyne Snodgrass argues for this, noting the word's normal sense. (2) The sleeper gets up to avoid shame: he will not be known as the man who disgraced the village's hospitality. Kenneth Bailey and others take it this way, so the point is God's own honor. Either way the parable argues from lesser to greater: if a sleepy neighbor gives, how much more God.

a: keep asking
p: The same three commands as in Matthew 7:7, here as the lesson of the friend at midnight.
b: Luke places the sayings shared with Matthew (Matthew 7:7–11) right after his own parable, so that "knock" picks up the friend knocking at midnight. The present-tense commands mean "keep on asking, keep on looking, keep on knocking." Seeking God and finding him is a promise of the Law and the prophets (Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13).

a: a snake in place of a fish
t: Fish and snake, egg and scorpion
p: Fish, bread and eggs were everyday food. A snake or scorpion is the cruel opposite.
b: Matthew pairs bread with a stone and fish with a snake (Matthew 7:9–10); Luke has fish with snake and egg with scorpion. Some suggest a snakelike fish, such as the scaleless catfish of the Sea of Galilee, which the Law counted unclean (Leviticus 11:10–12), and a white scorpion curled up like an egg. These guesses are possible but unproven. The force is plain without them: no father hands his hungry child something that will poison him. Snake and scorpion appear together again in 10:19.

a: the Father from heaven
t: The gift is the Holy Spirit
p: Where Matthew says the Father gives "what is good," Luke says he gives the Holy Spirit.
b: In Matthew 7:11 the Father gives "what is good to the people who ask him." Luke names the best gift of all: the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is one of Luke's great themes, from the births of John and Jesus (1:15, 35, 41, 67) to Pentecost and the church's mission (Acts 1:8; 2:1–4). In Acts the Spirit often comes to people who are praying (Acts 1:14; 4:31; 8:15). Whether believers should seek a later experience of the Spirit is debated among churches; see the card at Acts 2. Some manuscripts read "a good spirit" or "a good gift" (see the variant).

a: a demon that left a man unable to speak
p: The Greek word means deaf, mute, or both. Matthew tells a fuller form of the scene.
b: Kōphos can describe someone who cannot hear, cannot speak, or both. Luke tells the healing in one sentence and moves to the argument it started. Matthew has two such scenes: a speechless man (Matthew 9:32–34) and a man blind and speechless (Matthew 12:22–24), both followed by the charge that Jesus works with Beelzebul. In Mark the charge comes from scribes down from Jerusalem (Mark 3:22). Luke leaves the accusers vague: "some of them," from the crowd itself.

a: Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons
p: An old Canaanite title, "Baal the Prince," used here as a name for the chief of the demons.
b: The name goes back to Baal-zebub, god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), and to a Canaanite title known from Ugarit, zbl b'l, "Prince Baal." In Jesus' day it served as a name for Satan or a lord of demons. The KJV's "Beelzebub" comes from the Latin Vulgate and the Syriac. The accusation is serious: in Jewish law a person who led Israel astray by sorcery deserved death (Deuteronomy 13:1–5), and later Jewish and pagan critics said Jesus was a magician. See the note on Matthew 12:24.

a: a sign out of heaven
p: The demand will be answered at 11:29, the only sign this generation will get.
b: Luke splits the opponents in two: some explain the healing as sorcery (11:15), others want proof from heaven (11:16). Jesus answers the first group at once (11:17–26) and the second only later (11:29–32). A "sign out of heaven" meant something no magician could fake, such as fire from the sky or the sun standing still. To "test" him in this way is what Satan did in the wilderness (4:2; at 4:12 the compound ekpeirazō) and what Israel did to God (Deuteronomy 6:16).

a: house falls on house
p: The Greek says a house "falls on a house": a household turned against itself collapses.
b: Matthew and Mark speak of a kingdom and a house divided (Matthew 12:25; Mark 3:24–25). Luke's Greek is shorter and harder: oikos epi oikon piptei, "house falls upon house." It may mean that a divided family falls apart, or picture a city in ruins where one building collapses onto the next. Either way the logic is the same as in the other Gospels: if Satan's own power were driving out his demons, his kingdom would be destroying itself.
orig: οἶκος ἐπὶ οἶκον πίπτει (oikos epi oikon piptei)

a: your own sons
p: Other Jews drove out demons too. Josephus describes one, Eleazar, doing it before the future emperor Vespasian.
b: "Your sons" means people of your own, Jewish exorcists. Josephus tells how a Jew named Eleazar drew a demon out of a man's nose with a ring and a root prescribed by Solomon, in front of Vespasian and his officers (Antiquities 8.46–49). Acts 19:13–16 describes Jewish exorcists at Ephesus using Jesus' name. Jesus' argument is simple: if you do not call your own exorcists servants of Beelzebul, you cannot call me one. Those exorcists "will be your judges" of an unfair charge.

a: by God's finger
p: Pharaoh's magicians said of the plague of gnats, "It is the finger of God." Matthew has "God's Spirit."
b: When Moses' plague of gnats beat their arts, Pharaoh's magicians admitted: "It is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:19). The same finger wrote the Law on the stone tablets (Exodus 31:18). By using the phrase, Jesus sets his exorcisms beside the exodus: God is again freeing his people from a hostile power. Matthew 12:28 has "God's Spirit" instead. Most scholars think Luke's "finger" is the older wording, because Luke loves to speak of the Spirit and would hardly have removed it; a few think Luke chose the exodus image on purpose.

a: God's kingdom has already reached you
p: Is the kingdom present already, or still to come? This verse is the strongest case for "already."
b: Ephthasen means "has arrived, has caught up with." C. H. Dodd built his "realized eschatology" largely on this saying: in Jesus' deeds the kingdom is already here. Others stress that Jesus also teaches his disciples to pray "May your kingdom come" (11:2) and speaks of a future feast (13:28–29). Most scholars now hold both together: the kingdom is breaking in now through Jesus' works and will come in full later. Luke keeps this tension through the whole Gospel (17:20–21; 19:11; 21:31).

a: a stronger man comes against him
p: Isaiah asks whether loot can be taken from a warrior. John promised that a stronger one was coming.
b: Isaiah 49:24–25 asks, "Can loot be snatched from a warrior?" and answers that the LORD himself will take it back. John the Baptist announced "the one stronger than I am" (3:16, the same word ischyroteros). Luke's version is military: a palace or courtyard (aulē), full armor (panoplia, as in Ephesians 6:11), and the spoils divided, an echo of Isaiah 53:12. Mark pictures a burglar tying up a householder (Mark 3:27). Satan is the armed man; Jesus is the stronger one whose exorcisms are the loot.
r: Isaiah 49:24–25; Isaiah 53:12; 3:16; Mark 3:27; Matthew 12:29; Ephesians 6:11; Colossians 2:15

a: Anyone who is not on my side is against me
p: In 9:50 Jesus said the opposite about the outside exorcist. Both are true, aimed at different people.
b: In 9:50 Jesus told John not to stop a man driving out demons in his name, because whoever is not against them is for them. Here he says that whoever is not with him is against him. The two sayings answer different questions. The first warns disciples against jealousy toward others who work in Jesus' name. The second warns the onlookers that there is no neutral ground in the struggle with Satan. "Gather" and "scatter" are shepherd words (Ezekiel 34:12–13): Jesus is gathering God's scattered flock.

a: dry country
p: Jewish belief placed demons in deserts and ruins. In Tobit a demon flees to the far deserts of Egypt.
b: Waterless places were thought to be the homes of evil spirits. Isaiah pictures wild creatures and night demons in ruined Babylon and Edom (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). In Tobit the demon Asmodeus "fled up into the regions of Egypt" (Tobit 8:3). The goat for Azazel was sent into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:10). The story Jesus tells assumes this picture, then turns it into a warning about a life that is cleaned up but left empty.

a: seven more spirits
p: Seven means completeness. The end state is total possession, worse than before.
b: Seven is the Bible's number of fullness. Mary Magdalene had seven demons driven out (8:2). Here the empty house fills up with seven more. In Matthew the story ends "It will be like that for this evil generation, too" (Matthew 12:45), but Luke leaves it as a warning to individuals and sets it between the Beelzebul debate and the blessing on those who hear and keep the word of God (11:28). The point in Luke: being freed is not enough. The space must be filled by obedience to God's word.

a: Blessed is the womb that carried you
t: Blessing a son by blessing his mother
p: Praising a mother for her son was a Jewish way of praising the son himself.
b: The woman uses a familiar form of praise. In the Mishnah, Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai says of his pupil Joshua, "Happy is she who bore him" (Mishnah Avot 2:8). Jacob blesses Joseph with "blessings of breasts and womb" (Genesis 49:25). The scene also recalls Luke's first chapter, where Elizabeth calls Mary blessed and Mary sings that every generation will count her blessed (1:42, 45, 48). Only Luke tells this scene; it stands where Mark and Matthew tell of Jesus' mother and brothers (Mark 3:31–35).

a: Rather
p: The Greek menoun can correct ("No, rather") or agree and go further ("Yes, and more").
b: Menoun is a particle that can mean "on the contrary," "rather," or "yes indeed, but more than that." If it corrects, Jesus turns the woman away from honoring his mother toward obeying God. If it agrees and goes further, he includes Mary among those who hear and keep God's word, as Luke pictures her in 1:38, 45 and 2:19, 51. Translators divide: the KJV has "Yea rather," many modern versions "Blessed rather." How the churches read the verse is the subject of this chapter's card on Mary.

a: no sign except the sign of Jonah
t: What is the sign of Jonah?
p: In Matthew it is three days in the sea monster. In Luke it seems to be Jonah himself and his preaching.
b: Matthew explains the sign as Jonah's three days and nights in the fish, a picture of Jesus' burial (Matthew 12:40). Luke gives no such explanation. In Luke the sign is Jonah as the Ninevites met him: a prophet who came from far away, preached judgment, and was believed (11:30, 32). So the Son of Man, by his presence and preaching, is God's sign to this generation, and nothing more will be given. Many scholars think Luke's simpler form is older; others think he dropped Matthew's line. Some see the resurrection hinted at in Luke too, since Jonah came back from the deep.

a: the people of Nineveh
t: The repentance of Nineveh in Jewish memory
p: Nineveh's repentance was held up in synagogues on fast days as the model of true repentance.
b: Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, was Israel's fiercest enemy. Yet in the book of Jonah its king and people fasted and turned from violence, and God relented (Jonah 3:5–10). On public fast days, the Mishnah says, the elder told the people that Scripture does not say God saw Nineveh's sackcloth and fasting, but that "God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way" (Mishnah Taanit 2:1, citing Jonah 3:10). The book of Jonah is still read on Yom Kippur. Jesus uses the same story to shame his own hearers.

a: the queen from the south
t: The queen of Sheba at the judgment
p: A foreign queen crossed the world to hear Solomon. This generation will not listen to one greater.
b: The queen of Sheba came from southern Arabia to test Solomon with riddles (1 Kings 10:1–13; 2 Chronicles 9:1–12). Both witnesses Jesus names are Gentiles: a queen from the south and the people of Nineveh. At the judgment they will "be raised" (egerthēsetai, the resurrection verb) and stand as witnesses against Israel's own generation. Luke puts Solomon first and Jonah second, the reverse of Matthew, perhaps to keep the order of the Scriptures.

a: here is something greater than Solomon
p: The Greek is neuter: "something greater," not "someone greater."
b: Pleion is neuter, "more, something greater." It may point to Jesus himself without saying so outright, or to what is happening through him: God's kingdom, which outweighs Solomon's wisdom and Jonah's preaching. The same neuter appears in Matthew 12:6, "something greater than the temple." The understatement invites the hearer to finish the thought.

a: in a hidden corner
p: Luke's lamp lights the way for "people coming in", a Greek and Roman house with an entrance hall.
b: Matthew's lamp "shines for everyone in the house" (Matthew 5:15), the one room of a Galilean home. Luke's lamp is for "people coming in" (also 8:16), as in a larger Greek or Roman house where a lamp stood in the entrance. Kryptē is a cellar or hidden nook. Luke adapts the picture for his readers' homes. In this place the lamp answers the demand for a sign: God has not hidden the light; it is set up where all who come in can see it.

a: When your eye is sound
p: "Sound" is haplous, single or generous. An "evil eye" in Jewish speech was a grudging, stingy eye.
b: Haplous means simple, single, whole, and in ethics generous. In Jewish idiom an "evil eye" was envy and stinginess (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 23:6), while "the person with a kind eye" is the generous one (Proverbs 22:9). Matthew uses the saying in a passage about money (Matthew 6:22–23). Luke sets it after the sign of Jonah, so here the eye is the way a person takes in the light Jesus brings: those whose eye is sound see the sign; those whose eye is evil see only darkness.

a: it will be bright all through
p: The verse seems to say the same thing twice. Interpreters explain the repetition in more than one way.
b: Read flatly, the verse says "if your whole body is bright, it will be bright," and commentators have long called it a puzzle. Some find the difference in time: the person who lets the light in now ("is bright") will be wholly lit up later ("will be"), perhaps at the judgment. Others put the weight on the words "without a single dark part" and on the closing comparison: a life with no corner kept from God will shine as fully as a room in a lamp's blaze. Either way the point of 11:33–36 is the same: the light is there; take it in fully.

a: a Pharisee invited him
p: Only in Luke does Jesus dine in Pharisees' homes, three times.
b: Luke alone tells of Jesus eating with Pharisees (7:36; 11:37; 14:1). The Pharisees were a lay movement that took the purity laws of the priests into ordinary homes, so a shared table mattered greatly to them. Inviting a famous teacher was an honor and a test. Luke's picture of Pharisees is mixed: they invite Jesus, argue with him, warn him of Herod (13:31), and in Acts include Gamaliel and Christian believers (Acts 5:34; 15:5; 23:6–9). Readers should not flatten them into villains.

a: had not washed himself first
p: The verb is baptizō, "immerse, wash." Hand-washing before meals was a Pharisaic custom, not a law of Moses.
b: Luke writes ebaptisthē, "he was washed" or "immersed himself." Mark explains that Pharisees and many other Jews washed their hands before eating, by a tradition of the elders (Mark 7:3–4). The Torah required washing only for priests and for people who had become unclean; washing hands before ordinary meals was a pious extension of temple purity into the home, later set out in the Mishnah tractate Yadayim. Most think hand-washing is meant here, though some take the verb to mean full immersion.

a: the Lord
p: Luke often calls Jesus "the Lord" in his own narration, something Mark and Matthew almost never do.
b: Mark and Matthew use "the Lord" for Jesus mainly when people address him. Luke, telling the story after Easter, often uses ho kyrios, "the Lord," as his own name for Jesus (7:13, 19; 10:1, 39, 41; 11:39; 12:42; 13:15; 17:5–6; 22:61; 24:3). It reflects the church's confession that Jesus is Lord (Acts 2:36). Luke uses the same word for God (1:6, 9, 11), and the overlap is part of his message.

a: wash the outside of the cup and the plate clean
t: Inside and outside of a cup
p: Purity law treated a vessel's outside and inside separately. Jesus makes it a picture of the person.
b: Leviticus says a clay pot that becomes unclean must be broken (Leviticus 11:33). Later rules, gathered in the Mishnah tractate Kelim (25:1–9), treat the outer and inner surfaces of a vessel separately. Jacob Neusner argued that Jesus' saying reflects a real debate between the schools of Shammai and Hillel about which part of a cup made the rest unclean. Jesus turns the debate into a moral image: Pharisees care for the outside while their own inside is full of grabbing and wickedness. Compare Matthew 23:25–26.

a: give what is inside as alms
p: A puzzling command. The contents of the dishes, the heart, or an Aramaic misreading?
b: Ta enonta dote eleēmosynēn is unclear. (1) Give the contents of your cups and plates, the food, to the poor; then your meal is truly clean. (2) Give yourselves, your inner life, in mercy. (3) An old suggestion, followed by some Aramaic specialists, is that Aramaic dakkau, "cleanse," was read as zakkau, "give alms"; Matthew 23:26 has "start by washing the inside." Whatever its origin, Luke's text fits his book: alms to the poor show a clean heart (12:33; 19:8; Acts 9:36; 10:2, 4). A gloss gives the plain sense of "alms."
orig: τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην (ta enonta dote eleēmosynēn)

a: mint and rue and every garden plant
p: The Mishnah says rue did not have to be tithed. These Pharisees went beyond the rule.
b: The Law commands a tenth of the harvest for God (Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 14:22). Which crops counted was debated. Matthew lists mint, dill and cumin (Matthew 23:23). Luke has mint, rue and every garden plant. The Mishnah names rue among plants exempt from tithes (Mishnah Sheviit 9:1). So these Pharisees tithe more than the law asks. Jesus does not mock their care; "These you should have done." He objects to strictness about herbs alongside neglect of justice and the love of God.

a: justice and the love of God
t: Justice and the love of God
p: Luke's pair sums up the Law's two great commands, as in the lawyer's answer in 10:27.
b: Matthew has "justice, mercy and faithfulness" (Matthew 23:23), close to Micah 6:8. Luke has "justice and the love of God," which recalls the great commandment the lawyer quoted in 10:27 from Deuteronomy 6:5. "Love of God" can mean love for God or God's love; most take it as our love for God. Justice toward the neighbor and love for God: the two tables of the Law.

a: graves that no one can see
p: Touching a grave made a person unclean. Unmarked graves spread impurity without anyone knowing.
b: Under Numbers 19:16, anyone who touched a grave was unclean for seven days. So graves were marked: the Mishnah says that each year, a month before Passover, graves were marked so pilgrims would avoid them (Mishnah Shekalim 1:1). Matthew's version pictures whitewashed tombs, clean outside and rotten inside (Matthew 23:27). Luke's version is sharper: the Pharisees are like graves no one can see, so that people who trust them are made unclean without knowing it. The saying turns their own concern for purity against them.

a: lawyers
p: Not courtroom lawyers: experts in the law of Moses, Luke's word for scribes.
b: Nomikoi are experts in the nomos, the Law. Luke uses the word six times (7:30; 10:25; 11:45, 46, 52; 14:3), Matthew once (Matthew 22:35). They overlap with the scribes, who taught and applied the Law; many were Pharisees, but not all. Luke turns from the Pharisees as a lay movement (11:42–44) to the scholars who set the rules (11:46–52).

a: loads too heavy to carry
p: Did the scribes make life harder, or easier? The Pharisees saw their rules as making the Law livable.
b: Jesus charges the lawyers with laying burdens on people and not lifting a finger to help. Christian readers have long taken this to mean the whole Pharisaic system was crushing. Jewish scholars and many Christian ones, such as E. P. Sanders, point out that the Pharisees' interpretations often made the Law easier to keep in daily life, and that people respected them for it. The charge may target specific teachers who were strict with others and found ways out for themselves. Compare Acts 15:10, where Peter calls the Law itself a yoke.

a: You put up tombs for the prophets
p: Grand tombs in the Kidron Valley honored the heroes of Israel's past. Herod built a marble monument at David's tomb.
b: In Jesus' day Jerusalem's leaders honored the past with monumental tombs. Rock-cut tombs in the Kidron Valley, later called the tombs of Zechariah and Absalom, date from this period. Josephus says Herod built a costly white marble monument at the entrance to David's tomb (Antiquities 16.182). The Lives of the Prophets, a Jewish work probably of the first century AD, records where each prophet was buried. Jesus' irony: building tombs for murdered prophets finishes the work of the people who killed them.

a: God's Wisdom said
p: Who is quoted? No known book has these words. Matthew puts them in Jesus' own mouth.
b: No book in our Bibles or outside it contains this saying. Several answers are offered. (1) Jesus quotes a lost Jewish writing. (2) "God's Wisdom" is a reverent way of saying "God in his wisdom decided." (3) Jesus speaks as Wisdom herself, the figure of Proverbs 8 and the Wisdom of Solomon, who "in every generation passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27); Matthew 23:34 has Jesus say "I am sending you prophets." Luke has already spoken of Wisdom's children (7:35).
r: Matthew 23:34; 7:35; Proverbs 8:1–36; Wisdom of Solomon 7:27; Proverbs 1:20–33

a: apostles
p: Apostolos means "someone sent." Luke's readers would think of the apostles of Acts.
b: Apostolos means someone sent with a message. In Wisdom's saying it may have meant messengers in general, but for Luke the word means the Twelve and other witnesses of Acts (6:13; Acts 1:26; 14:14). Acts tells how some were hunted and killed: Stephen (Acts 7), James (Acts 12:2), and Paul's sufferings. Jesus himself is the last of the prophets killed in Jerusalem (13:33–34).

a: called to account for the blood of every prophet
p: The verb ekzēteō, "seek out, demand," is the word of God avenging blood, as in Genesis 9 and 2 Chronicles 24.
b: The Greek is literally "so that the blood ... may be sought from this generation." It echoes God's words after the flood, "I will demand a reckoning" for human blood (Genesis 9:5), and the dying prayer of Zechariah: "May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out" (2 Chronicles 24:22). The generation that rejects the last and greatest messenger fills up the whole history of rejection. Luke expects this judgment to fall in the war of AD 66–70 (19:41–44; 21:20–24).

a: from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah
p: The first murder in the Bible and the last in the usual Hebrew order, from Genesis to Chronicles.
b: Abel's blood cried out from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada, was stoned "in the courtyard of the LORD's house" on King Joash's order (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). In the order given by the Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) and in most printed Hebrew Bibles, Chronicles comes last, so "from Abel to Zechariah" would mean from the first book to the last, like "from A to Z." The great medieval codices, Aleppo and Leningrad, put Chronicles first among the Writings instead. Many scholars see in Jesus' words evidence that Chronicles already stood last in his day; others think the order was not yet fixed and that he simply named the first and last murders of righteous men in the story. Luke has no father's name; on Matthew's "son of Berechiah" see the note on Matthew 23:35.

a: between the altar and the house
p: "The house" is the sanctuary. Later Jewish legend said Zechariah's blood kept boiling until the Babylonians came.
b: "The house" means God's house, the sanctuary itself; the altar of burnt offering stood in the courtyard in front of it. Jewish tradition remembered this murder as a great sin. The Babylonian Talmud (Gittin 57b; Sanhedrin 96b) and Lamentations Rabbah tell that when the Babylonian general Nebuzaradan entered the temple, he found Zechariah's blood still seething, and could not quiet it until he had slaughtered many in Jerusalem. The legend shows how close Jesus' words are to Jewish reflection on the fall of Jerusalem.

a: the key to knowledge
p: The lawyers held the key to Scripture's meaning and locked others out. The Gospel of Thomas has a close parallel.
b: A key opens the door into understanding God's word, and so into the kingdom (Matthew 23:13 says they "lock up the kingdom"). Scribes were the keepers of interpretation. Jesus charges that their way of reading kept people from seeing what the Scriptures pointed to. The Gospel of Thomas, saying 39, has a similar form: the Pharisees and scribes have taken the keys of knowledge and hidden them. In Luke the key is restored at the end, when the risen Jesus opens the Scriptures to his disciples (24:27, 32, 45).

a: draw him out with questions
p: The verbs are hunting words: they lie in ambush to catch a word from his mouth.
b: Apostomatizein means to make someone speak off the cuff, to draw out an answer they can use. Enedreuontes is "lying in ambush" and thēreusai "to hunt, to catch." The meal that began with an invitation ends in open hostility. Luke prepares for the trap questions in the temple (20:20–26). The same Gospel will also show Pharisees warning Jesus of danger (13:31), so Luke does not make every Pharisee an enemy.

a: by the tens of thousands
p: The Greek myriades means "tens of thousands," a deliberate exaggeration for a huge crowd.
b: A myrias is ten thousand, and the plural is Luke's way of saying "countless" (compare Acts 21:20). The crowd is so dense that people tread on one another. The scene sets up the chapter: Jesus speaks first to his disciples (12:1–12), then to someone from the crowd (12:13–21), then to the disciples again (12:22–53), then to the crowds (12:54–59). Luke's Jesus teaches his followers in the hearing of all, so the crowd overhears what discipleship costs.

a: the yeast of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy
p: Yeast spreads through the whole batch. Luke names this yeast plainly: hypocrisy.
b: A little yeast works through all the dough, so it was a common picture of a spreading influence, usually a bad one; Passover required every trace of it to be removed (Exodus 12:15; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). In Mark the warning is against "the yeast of the Pharisees and the yeast of Herod" (Mark 8:15); in Matthew it means their teaching (Matthew 16:6, 12). Luke defines it as hypokrisis, play-acting, a gap between outside and inside, as at the Pharisee's table (11:39–44). The warning is aimed at the disciples, who can catch it too.
r: Mark 8:15; Matthew 16:6; Matthew 16:12; Exodus 12:15; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Galatians 5:9; 11:39–44

a: shouted from the rooftops
p: Houses had flat roofs. Public announcements were called out from them.
b: Village houses had flat roofs reached by an outside stair, used for drying crops, sleeping in summer and calling to neighbors (compare 5:19; Acts 10:9). A message called from a roof reached the whole village. In Matthew 10:27 the disciples are told to shout from the rooftops what Jesus whispered to them. Luke has the same verb, kēryssō, "announce, proclaim," but in the passive, and his form is a warning: what you whispered behind closed doors (tameia, the inner storerooms) will be made public. Hypocrisy cannot stay hidden.

a: My friends
p: Only here in the first three Gospels does Jesus call his disciples "my friends."
b: The address tois philois mou is unique in Matthew, Mark and Luke, though John has Jesus say, "I call you friends" (John 15:14–15). It comes just before a warning of persecution and death. Friendship was a prized bond in the Greek world, a relationship of loyalty unto death. Jesus speaks to those who will be in danger for his sake, and offers them his friendship along with God's care (12:6–7).

a: Fear the One who has authority
p: Almost every reader takes this to be God. A few have argued for the devil.
b: The one to fear is the one with authority after death to cast into Gehenna. Nearly all interpreters, ancient and modern, take this as God, the judge of all, whose power goes beyond death. A minority have suggested the devil, on the grounds that Jesus would not tell friends to be afraid of God. But Scripture does not set God's fatherly care against the fear of God (Proverbs 1:7): two verses later the same God counts the hairs on their heads. Proper fear of God drives out fear of human beings.

a: throw people into Gehenna
p: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem. English Bibles usually write "hell."
b: Geenna comes from Hebrew Gê Hinnōm, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where kings of Judah had burned children to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31; 2 Kings 23:10). The prophets made it a place of judgment, and by Jesus' time Jewish writers used its name for the place of fiery punishment after death. This is the only place Luke uses the word. Whether Gehenna means endless punishment or final destruction is debated; see the note and card at Matthew 10:28. A gloss gives "the fire of hell."

a: Five sparrows sell for two small coins
p: Sparrows were the cheapest food in the market. Buy two pairs and get a fifth bird free.
b: Small birds were sold, plucked and roasted, as poor people's meat. Matthew has two sparrows for one assarion, a small copper coin (Matthew 10:29); Luke has five for two. Many commentators note that buying two coins' worth seems to have brought an extra bird thrown in. Even that fifth bird, worth nothing at all, is not forgotten by God. The argument goes from the least to the greatest.

a: the Son of Man too will declare for that person
t: Jesus and the Son of Man
p: Jesus speaks of "me" and of "the Son of Man" in the same breath. Is he one and the same?
b: Matthew's version has "I too will declare" (Matthew 10:32). Luke keeps "the Son of Man." Rudolf Bultmann and some others thought Jesus was speaking of a heavenly figure other than himself, whom the church later identified with him. Most scholars read it as Jesus' own way of speaking of himself in the third person, with the Son of Man as judge in God's court (Daniel 7:13–14). In Acts Stephen sees "the Son of Man standing at God's right hand" as his witness (Acts 7:56).

a: the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven
t: The sin against the Spirit in Luke
p: In Mark and Matthew this follows the Beelzebul charge. Luke puts it among warnings to disciples facing trial.
b: Mark and Matthew place the saying right after the scribes say Jesus has Beelzebul (Mark 3:28–30; Matthew 12:31–32). Luke puts it here, between denying Jesus (12:9) and the Spirit's help at trial (12:12). In this setting, speaking against the Son of Man may mean the misunderstanding of people before Easter, or a disciple's moment of weakness like Peter's (22:54–62), which can be forgiven. Rejecting the Spirit's witness through the apostles (Acts 5:3, 9; 7:51) is more serious. What the sin is remains debated among the churches; see the card at Matthew 12:31–32.

a: before synagogues and rulers and authorities
p: Acts tells how this came true: Peter and John before the council, Stephen, Paul before governors and a king.
b: Synagogues held local courts that could order a beating (2 Corinthians 11:24). "Rulers and authorities" covers Jewish and Roman officials alike. Acts fulfills the promise step by step: Peter, "filled with the Holy Spirit," answers the council (Acts 4:8); Stephen's opponents "were no match for the wisdom and the Spirit he spoke with" (Acts 6:10); Paul defends himself before Felix, Festus and Agrippa (Acts 24–26). Luke 21:12–15 repeats the promise in the discourse on the end.
r: Acts 4:8; Acts 6:10; Acts 24:10; Acts 26:1–2; 21:12–15; Mark 13:11; Matthew 10:17–20; 2 Corinthians 11:24

a: split our inheritance with me
p: Rabbis were often asked to settle inheritance cases. The older brother received a double share.
b: Under the Law, the firstborn son received a double share of his father's estate (Deuteronomy 21:17), and brothers often kept the land together rather than divide it. A younger brother might want his part to live on. People asked respected teachers to arbitrate such cases, and the Mishnah has a whole tractate on inheritance law (Bava Batra 8–9). The man does not ask Jesus what is just. He asks Jesus to take his side. Compare the younger son in 15:12, who asks for his share too early.

a: who put me in charge as judge or divider over you?
p: The words echo the challenge to Moses: "Who put you as a chief and a judge over us?"
b: When Moses tried to settle a quarrel between two Hebrews, one of them retorted, "Who put you as a chief and a judge over us?" (Exodus 2:14). Stephen quotes the same words in Acts 7:27, 35. Here Jesus asks the question himself, to refuse the role. He has not come to divide property but to warn against the greed that sets brothers against each other. "Man" (Anthrōpe) is a cool, distancing address, as in 22:58, 60.

a: every kind of greed
p: Pleonexia is the desire to have more, more than one's share.
b: Pleonexia comes from pleon echein, "to have more." It is the itch for more than enough. Paul calls it a kind of idolatry (Colossians 3:5; Ephesians 5:5), and it closes the list of things that come out of the heart in Mark 7:22. Jesus' point in the second half of the verse is that life (zōē) does not come out of possessions, even when they overflow. The parable that follows shows a man who forgets this.

a: he argued it out with himself
t: A man alone with his soul
p: The rich man talks only to himself. In Luke's parables, inner speeches reveal the heart.
b: Several of Luke's parables let us hear a character's thoughts: the prodigal son (15:17–19), the dishonest manager (16:3–4), the unjust judge (18:4–5), the vineyard owner (20:13). The rich man consults no family, workers or friends; he talks to his own soul. Kenneth Bailey notes that in a Middle Eastern village such decisions were discussed endlessly with others. Count the words "my" and "I": my crops, my barns, my grain, my goods, my soul. His world has shrunk to himself.

a: Eat, drink, celebrate
p: Ecclesiastes commends eating and drinking as God's gift. Sirach describes a rich man just like this one.
b: Ecclesiastes says, "There is nothing good for a person under the sun except to eat and drink and be glad" (Ecclesiastes 8:15), but always as a gift from God for the days God gives. Isaiah 22:13 quotes the reckless: "Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!" The closest parallel is Sirach 11:18–19: a man grows rich by care and thrift and says, "I have found rest, and now I will eat from my goods," not knowing how soon he will leave them to others and die. 1 Enoch 97:8–10 has a similar woe on the rich.
r: Ecclesiastes 8:15; Ecclesiastes 2:18–21; Isaiah 22:13; Sirach 11:18–19; 1 Enoch 97:8–10; 1 Corinthians 15:32

a: Fool!
p: The fool in Scripture is not stupid but godless: he lives as if there were no God.
b: Aphrōn means senseless. In the Greek Psalms it renders the fool who says to himself there is no God (Psalm 14:1; 53:1). The rich man is a practical atheist: he plans as if his life were his own. God, who has not been in his thoughts, speaks the only words addressed to him in the story. Jesus used the same word for the Pharisees in 11:40.

a: they demand your soul back from you
p: The verb means to demand repayment of a loan. "They" is a reverent way of saying God.
b: Apaitousin is used of calling in a debt or reclaiming something lent. The man's soul, his life, was never his property; it was on loan. The plural "they" is a Jewish way of avoiding God's name (compare 6:38; 16:9), though some think of angels sent to take the soul. The play on "soul" runs through the passage: he speaks to his soul (12:19), his soul is reclaimed (12:20), and Jesus tells the disciples not to worry about their soul, that is, their life (12:22–23).

a: is not rich toward God
p: What makes someone rich toward God? Luke's answer comes a few verses later: give to the poor.
b: The phrase is not explained in the parable itself. Luke answers it in 12:33: "Sell your property and give alms ... an endless treasure in the heavens." Being rich toward God means using wealth in God's way, above all for the poor. The parable does not condemn harvests, barns or planning. It condemns a life that treats a good harvest as private security, with no thought for God or for others. Basil of Caesarea, preaching on this parable during a famine, told the rich that the bread they stored belonged to the hungry.

a: stop worrying about your life
t: The same teaching, a different setting
p: Matthew sets these words in the Sermon on the Mount. Luke sets them after the rich fool.
b: Luke 12:22–31 runs closely with Matthew 6:25–33, often word for word in the Greek, and this translation keeps Matthew's wording where the Greek agrees. The settings differ. In Matthew the words are part of the great sermon. In Luke they follow the rich fool: the rich man worried about where to store too much; the disciples are not to worry about having too little. Both trust or distrust God with what they own.

a: Think about the ravens
p: Matthew has "the wild birds." Luke names ravens, birds the Law called unclean, and the Psalms say God feeds.
b: Ravens were unclean birds under the Law (Leviticus 11:15), scavengers no one would keep. Yet Scripture says God feeds them: "Who has the raven's meal ready / when its chicks call to God for help" (Job 38:41), and "the raven's chicks what they cry out for" (Psalm 147:9). Ravens fed Elijah (1 Kings 17:4–6). If God provides for birds without storerooms or barns, unlike the rich fool who built bigger barns, he will provide for his own.

a: add a cubit to the length of your life
p: The Greek word can mean a person's age or height. Most read a cubit added to a life as a little more time.
b: Hēlikia means a person's time of life, and also height (Zacchaeus is short in hēlikia at 19:3; Jesus grows in it at 2:52). A cubit, about a foot and a half, measures length, so some read the saying as adding to one's height. Most scholars take it as lifespan pictured as a length: no one can stretch a life even a little by worrying. Luke's next verse calls this "the smallest thing" (12:26), which fits a little more time better than a foot and a half of height. The fuller discussion is at Matthew 6:27.

a: tossed into the oven
p: Dried grass and wildflowers were cheap fuel for the clay oven.
b: Wood was scarce in Galilee. Women heated the clay bread oven with dried grass, thorn bushes and dung. The wildflowers that are lovelier than Solomon's robes one day are fuel the next. For the lilies, see the note on Matthew 6:28.

a: do not be left up in the air
p: Meteōrizesthai means to be raised in the air, and so to hang in suspense, anxious.
b: The verb comes from the same root as English "meteor": things up in the air. In other Greek writers it means being puffed up with pride, or tossed like a ship on high waves, and in papyrus letters it means being anxious or unsettled. Here it sums up the worry Jesus has been describing: a mind that cannot come to rest. The KJV's "neither be ye of doubtful mind" catches part of the sense.

a: The nations of the world
p: A Jewish phrase for the non-Jewish peoples, common in later rabbinic writing as umot ha'olam.
b: Matthew has "the Gentiles" (Matthew 6:32). Luke's "the nations of the world" matches a phrase that rabbinic writings use often, umot ha'olam, for the peoples outside Israel. The contrast is not ethnic pride but trust: people who do not know God as Father must chase food and clothing; those who do know him can let the Father take care of it. Luke, writing largely for Gentile believers, keeps the Jewish phrasing of Jesus' words.

a: little flock
p: God as shepherd of a small flock, and Daniel's promise that the kingdom will be given to God's people.
b: The prophets picture God as a shepherd gathering his scattered flock: "Like a shepherd he will graze his flock" (Isaiah 40:11; Ezekiel 34:11–16). Daniel sees the kingdom given to "the holy ones of the Most High" (Daniel 7:18, 27). Jesus' disciples are a tiny flock among wolves (10:3), but the kingdom is theirs because the Father has gladly chosen to give it. The verb eudokēsen is the one used at Jesus' baptism for God's delight in his Son (3:22).

a: Sell your property and give alms
p: Did Jesus mean all disciples, some disciples, or a spirit of generosity?
b: Luke's Gospel presses this command hard (14:33; 18:22), and Acts shows the first believers selling property to share (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–37). Readings differ. (1) It is meant literally for all, as for the Franciscans and some radical movements. (2) It is a special call for some, the "counsels of perfection" of monastic tradition. (3) It describes a free and generous spirit toward wealth; Acts itself shows believers who still own homes (Acts 12:12). The churches' views are compared at Matthew 19:21 and Acts 4.

a: Have your robes tucked into your belts
p: Long robes were tucked into a belt to work, run or travel, as Israel ate the first Passover.
b: The Greek says "let your waists be girded." A long robe was pulled up and tucked under the belt to leave the legs free. Israel was to eat the Passover "your waist wrapped for travel, your sandals on your feet" (Exodus 12:11), ready to leave at once. Elijah tucked up his robe to run before Ahab's chariot (1 Kings 18:46). With burning lamps added, the picture is of servants ready through the night. Compare the young women with their lamps in Matthew 25:1–13.

a: he will tie up his own robe, have them recline for the meal, and come over and serve them
p: No master in that world served his slaves at table. This one will.
b: In 17:7–9 Jesus asks which master would tell a slave just in from the field to sit down and eat. None would. Yet here the master tucks up his own robe, seats the watchful slaves and waits on them. The picture breaks the ordinary world apart, as God's kingdom does. At the Last Supper Jesus says that in their company he is like the one who waits on tables (22:27), and John shows him tying on a towel to wash his disciples' feet (John 13:4–5). The end of the age is pictured as a banquet where the Lord himself serves.

a: the second watch of the night, or even the third
p: The night was divided into watches. The latest watches are when sleepy servants are most likely to fail.
b: Romans divided the night into four watches of about three hours (Mark 13:35 names all four). Older Israelite practice knew three, as in Gideon's "middle watch" (Judges 7:19). Luke names the second and third, the deep middle of the night. A master home from a wedding feast late at night is the test: will his servants still be awake?

a: dig his way into his house
p: Houses were built of mud brick or rough stone. Burglars broke in by digging through the wall.
b: The verb diorussō means to dig through. The Law speaks of a thief "caught tunneling in" at night (Exodus 22:2), and Job of one who "digs through into houses" in the dark (Job 24:16). The picture of the Lord's coming "like a thief" became common in the early church (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 3:3; 16:15). Some manuscripts add "he would have stayed awake," as in Matthew (see the variant).
r: Exodus 22:2; Job 24:16; Matthew 24:43; 1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 3:3; Revelation 16:15

a: The Son of Man comes at an hour you are not counting on
p: Most read this as Jesus' return at the end. Others think of the judgment of AD 70, or of each person's death.
b: Christians have mostly read the parables of 12:35–48 about the Second Coming, delayed beyond what the first disciples expected (12:45). Preterist readers apply them to the coming of the Son of Man in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. Some, like the rich fool's story just before, read them as the call to be ready for death, which comes on its own unknown night (12:20). The text stresses readiness, not dates (Acts 1:7). On the views of the end, see the card at Matthew 24.

a: Peter asked
p: Only Luke has Peter's question. Jesus' answer points to leaders: the manager over the household.
b: Peter asks whether the parable is for the disciples or for all. Jesus answers with a question about a manager (oikonomos), a slave set over the rest of the household to feed them. In Matthew the same parable has a "slave" (Matthew 24:45). Luke's word fits leaders in the church, who are "managers of God's mysteries" and must be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Titus 1:7; 1 Peter 4:10). Those with more responsibility face a stricter accounting (12:47–48).

a: I tell you truly
p: Matthew has "Amen, I tell you." Luke writes the Greek word "truly."
b: Matthew 24:47 has amēn legō hymin. Luke often keeps Jesus' Hebrew "amen" (12:37 just before), but sometimes replaces it with Greek alēthōs, "truly" (9:27; 21:3), or nai, "yes" (11:51). The translation keeps the difference so readers can see Luke's choice.

a: He will cut him in two
p: A savage punishment, or a Semitic way of saying "cut him off"?
b: Dichotomeō literally means to cut in two, a known punishment in the ancient world (compare Susanna 55, 59 in the Greek Daniel). But the slave then receives "his share with the unfaithful," which assumes he is still alive. So many scholars think the word stands for a Hebrew or Aramaic expression for being cut off from the community, as in the Dead Sea Scrolls' rules for expelling members. Luke's "the unfaithful" (Matthew has "the hypocrites") fits a steward who was trusted and failed. See the note on Matthew 24:51.

a: will get a heavy beating
p: The Law weighed sins done in knowledge more heavily than sins of ignorance. So does Jesus.
b: The Law distinguished sins done unintentionally, which an offering could atone for, from sins done "with a high hand," in open defiance (Numbers 15:27–31). Deuteronomy limits a beating to "the number of blows his wrong deserves" (Deuteronomy 25:2). Jesus applies the principle to the judgment: the slave who knew and refused is punished more than the one who did not know. Christian theologians have drawn from these verses the idea of degrees of reward and punishment (compare 10:12–14; 20:47).

a: When someone is given a lot, a lot will be looked for from him
p: A principle with a long life in English speech. The Wisdom of Solomon says the mighty will be mightily tested.
b: The proverb sums up the parable: trust brings accountability. The Wisdom of Solomon warns kings that the least may be pardoned out of mercy, "but the mighty will be examined mightily" (Wisdom of Solomon 6:6). The saying has become a common English proverb, often quoted by presidents and in commencement speeches, usually in the KJV's form, "unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required."

a: I came to cast fire upon the earth
p: Fire of judgment, fire of the Spirit, or the fire of conflict? John promised a baptism "with the Holy Spirit and fire."
b: John the Baptist said the one coming would baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire, and burn the chaff (3:16–17). Fire in Scripture stands for judgment (Genesis 19:24; Malachi 4:1), purifying (Malachi 3:2–3), and God's presence; at Pentecost the Spirit comes as "tongues that looked like fire" (Acts 2:3). In context, the fire divides families (12:51–53). Jesus longs for it but must first pass through his own "baptism." The Gospel of Thomas has similar sayings (10, 82, "Whoever is near me is near the fire").
r: 3:16–17; Acts 2:3; Malachi 3:2–3; 9:54; Gospel of Thomas 10; Gospel of Thomas 82

a: how I wish it were already burning
orig: τί θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη (ti thelō ei ēdē anēphthē)
p: The Greek is terse. Most read a longing; older translations read a question.
b: Word for word the clause runs "and what do I want, if already it was kindled." Most scholars take ti as "how" and ei as "that," as Greek can after verbs of wishing, which gives the longing this translation follows. The KJV reads a question: "what will I, if it be already kindled?" Others punctuate it as "what more do I want, if it is already kindled?", as if the fire has already begun in Jesus' ministry. The next verse favors the note of longing: Jesus is "hard pressed" until his baptism is carried out (12:50).

a: there is a baptism I must be baptized with
p: Jesus has already been baptized in the Jordan. This baptism is his coming suffering and death.
b: In Mark, Jesus asks James and John whether they can be baptized with the baptism he is baptized with (Mark 10:38–39). Being "plunged" was a picture of being overwhelmed by disaster: "Save me, God, for the water has reached my throat" (Psalm 69:1). Synechomai, "hard pressed," means held in, gripped (Paul uses it in Philippians 1:23). Jesus feels the weight of what is coming in Jerusalem (9:51; 22:42–44). Paul later links Christian baptism with Jesus' death (Romans 6:3–4).

a: father against son and son against father
p: The words come from Micah 7:6. Jewish tradition read that verse as a sign of the days before the Messiah.
b: Micah 7:6 describes a society falling apart: son against father, daughter against mother, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law. The Mishnah quotes Micah 7:6 among the signs of the time "in the footsteps of the Messiah" (Mishnah Sotah 9:15). Luke's angel had promised that John would "turn fathers' hearts back to their children" (1:17, from Malachi 4:6); now Jesus warns that loyalty to him will split households. Luke's balanced pairs, three against two and two against three, show the split runs both ways. See the note on Matthew 10:35.

a: a cloud coming up over the west
p: In the land of Israel, clouds from the Mediterranean bring rain; the south wind brings desert heat.
b: The Mediterranean lies west of the land, so clouds rising there mean rain, as Elijah's servant saw "a little cloud ... coming up out of the sea" (1 Kings 18:44). A wind from the south blows off the desert and brings scorching heat. Matthew's version uses a red sky at evening and morning (Matthew 16:2–3). Ordinary farmers read these signs well. Jesus' complaint is that they will not read the far plainer signs of God's time in what he is doing.

a: this moment
p: Kairos is time as opportunity, the decisive moment, not time on the clock.
b: Greek has chronos for time as duration and kairos for the right or decisive time. "This kairos" is the moment of Jesus' ministry, the time of God's visiting. As he weeps over Jerusalem, Jesus will say the city did not recognize the time when God came to it (19:44, kairos again). Calling the crowds "hypocrites" here means they could read these signs if they wanted to.

a: the judge will turn you over to the bailiff
p: The praktor was the court officer who collected debts. A debtor could be jailed until paid.
b: The praktōr was an official, known from Greek and Egyptian papyri, who enforced court judgments, seized property and kept debtors in prison until the debt was paid. Matthew 5:25–26 uses the saying about making peace with a brother. Luke places it after the call to read the times: the hearers are on their way to court with God, and should settle now, while there is time. A similar picture of debtors in prison appears in Matthew 18:30, 34.

a: the last tiny coin
p: Tertullian read the prison as the place of the dead, where small sins are paid off. Most read it as a parable of urgency.
b: The lepton was the smallest coin in use (two of them are the widow's gift in 21:2). The point of the saying is urgency: settle now, or pay everything. Some early writers read it further. Tertullian took the prison to be the world of the dead, where the soul pays even for small faults before the resurrection (On the Soul 58), and later Catholic teaching on purgatory cited such texts among others. Most Protestant and many Catholic interpreters read it simply as a warning to repent before judgment. The churches' views are compared at Matthew 12:32.

a: Pilate had mixed their blood with their sacrifices
p: No other source mentions this killing. It fits what Josephus and Philo say of Pilate.
b: Only Luke records this event. The Galileans were apparently killed while offering sacrifices in the temple courts, most likely at Passover, the one feast when lay Israelites slaughtered their own lambs (Mishnah Pesahim 5:5–6). Pontius Pilate governed Judea AD 26–36. Josephus tells of his clashes with the Jews: the army standards brought into Jerusalem, a riot over temple money spent on an aqueduct, in which soldiers clubbed many to death, and the slaughter of Samaritans at Mount Gerizim that ended his rule (Antiquities 18.55–62, 85–89). Philo quotes a letter calling him cruel and given to executions without trial (Embassy to Gaius 302).

a: greater sinners than every other Galilean
p: Many believed that suffering showed sin. Jesus refuses that reasoning, but does not let his hearers off.
b: The belief that disaster proves guilt runs deep: Job's friends argued it (Job 4:7–8), and the disciples ask in John 9:2 whose sin caused a man's blindness. Jesus answers no. The victims were not worse than anyone else. But he immediately turns the question back on the questioners: they are not safer than the victims, and they too must repent. The passage refuses both easy answers: that sufferers deserve it, and that the rest of us are fine.

a: you will all perish the same way
p: A warning of final judgment, or of the war with Rome, when Jews died in the temple courts and under falling walls?
b: "The same way" (homoiōs; in 13:5 hōsautōs) can be read loosely: you will all perish too, in the judgment. N. T. Wright and others read it more literally as a warning about the revolt against Rome: in AD 66–70 many Jews were cut down by Roman swords in the temple courts and crushed under Jerusalem's falling buildings, as Josephus describes. Luke surely knew of that war (19:41–44; 21:20–24). The two readings can stand together: the coming disaster is a picture of the judgment that repentance escapes.

a: the tower at Siloam
p: Siloam was in the southeast of Jerusalem by the Pool of Siloam. No other record of the collapse survives.
b: Siloam lay at the south end of the City of David, where Hezekiah's tunnel brought water to the Pool of Siloam (John 9:7). Nehemiah mentions "the wall of the Pool of Shelah," the same place (Nehemiah 3:15). A tower in the city wall there may have collapsed. Some have guessed it was linked with Pilate's aqueduct works, but there is no evidence. The large stepped pool of the Herodian period was found by archaeologists in 2004.

a: bigger debtors
p: "Debtors" here means sinners, as in the Lord's Prayer (11:4).
b: Jesus changes words between the two examples: the Galileans were not greater "sinners" (13:2); those killed by the tower were not greater "debtors" (opheiletai). The second word reflects the Aramaic use of "debt" for sin that lies behind the Lord's Prayer (11:4; Matthew 6:12) and the parable of the two debtors (7:41–43). Sin is a debt owed to God.

a: a fig tree that had been planted in his vineyard
p: The prophets pictured Israel as a vine and a fig tree. Luke tells this parable instead of Mark's cursing of the fig tree.
b: Isaiah's song of the vineyard asks why God's vineyard produced bad grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7). Micah and Jeremiah lament that there are no figs (Micah 7:1; Jeremiah 8:13), and Hosea compares Israel's ancestors to early figs (Hosea 9:10). Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. Mark and Matthew tell of Jesus cursing a fig tree near Jerusalem (Mark 11:12–14, 20–21; Matthew 21:18–20); Luke has no such scene. Many scholars think this parable takes its place, with a striking difference: here the tree is given more time.
r: Isaiah 5:1–7; Micah 7:1; Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Mark 11:12–14; Matthew 21:18–20; 3:9

a: three years running
p: The Law forbade eating a new tree's fruit for three years. Three more fruitless years means a hopeless tree.
b: Leviticus says the fruit of a newly planted tree must not be eaten for three years; in the fourth it is holy to the LORD, and from the fifth the owner may eat (Leviticus 19:23–25). So if the owner has looked for fruit for three years now, the tree is well past the age when it should bear. Many readers since the church fathers have also heard the three years of Jesus' ministry, though Luke does not count his ministry in years. The point is patience that has run out.

a: give it this one year more
t: A tree begging for another year
p: The ancient Story of Ahiqar has a tree that begs to be spared one more year. The verdict there is the opposite.
b: In the Syriac form of the Story of Ahiqar, a wise man rebukes his treacherous nephew with a fable: a palm tree by a river gave its owner no fruit, and when he came to cut it down, it begged to be left one more year, promising to bear carobs. The owner refused. Commentators have long noted the parallel. The tale was widely known, but the likeness is only in the picture. In Jesus' parable the worker pleads for the tree and the year of grace is granted, with extra care: digging and manure.

a: If not, you can chop it down
p: We never learn whether the tree bore fruit. The hearers must supply the ending.
b: The Greek breaks off: "and if it bears fruit in the future ..." without finishing the thought, then "but if not, you will cut it down." This translation supplies one word, "good," where the gardener leaves the sentence hanging. The parable stops before the year is up. John the Baptist had warned that the ax already lay against the root (3:9). This is a parable of mercy and urgency at once: God's patience gives more time, but not unlimited time. Christian readers have seen in the vineyard worker a picture of Christ interceding (compare 22:32; 23:34), Jewish readers a picture of Moses or Abraham pleading for the people.

a: One Sabbath Jesus was teaching in a synagogue
p: This is the last time Luke shows Jesus in a synagogue.
b: Luke's account of Jesus' public work began with a Sabbath in the Nazareth synagogue (4:16–30), where he read Isaiah's promise of release for captives. It ends its synagogue scenes here, with a woman released from bondage on a Sabbath. The two scenes frame Jesus' work: the word of release announced (4:18) and acted out (13:12, 16). After this Jesus teaches in homes, on the road and finally in the temple (19:47).

a: a spirit of weakness
p: Luke describes her illness as a spirit. Jesus does not drive out a demon; he lays hands on her.
b: Pneuma astheneias, "a spirit of weakness," is a Semitic way of describing a disabling condition, here caused, Jesus says, by Satan's binding (13:16). Yet the story is not told as an exorcism: Jesus speaks a word of release and lays his hands on her. Modern readers have guessed at a spinal condition, but the text gives no medical diagnosis. "At all" (eis to panteles) may go with "could not" or with "upright": she could not stand up fully, or could not stand up at all.

a: you have been released
p: One verb family runs through the scene: released, untie, tied up, untied. Jesus' answer turns on it.
b: Jesus tells her, apolelysai, "you have been released." In his reply he asks whether the critics do not lyei, "untie," an ox on the Sabbath (13:15), and says that Satan edēsen, "tied up," this woman, who had to be lythēnai, "untied" (13:16). The argument is built on the word: if an animal may be untied for a drink on the Sabbath, how much more a daughter of Abraham from Satan's rope. In 4:18 Jesus announced "release" (aphesis) for captives.

a: synagogue leader
p: The archisynagogos ran the synagogue's meetings and chose who would read and teach.
b: The archisynagōgos was a respected local man who looked after the building and arranged the services: who would read Scripture, pray and preach (Acts 13:15). Inscriptions show the title across the Jewish world, including the Theodotus inscription found in Jerusalem. Jairus held the same office (8:41).

a: Six days are given us when work must be done
p: Saving a life overrode the Sabbath. Healing a long illness that could wait one more day was another matter.
b: The leader quotes the commandment: "You have six days to work and get all your jobs done" (Deuteronomy 5:13). Jewish teachers agreed that danger to life overrides the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). Treating a chronic condition was not urgent, so it could wait. The leader's rule is reasonable by those standards, and he speaks to the crowd, not to Jesus. Jesus answers that this woman's release is exactly what the Sabbath is for: a day of rest from bondage (Deuteronomy 5:15).

a: set his ox or donkey loose from the manger
p: Everyone let animals drink on the Sabbath. The strict Damascus Document set tight limits on how.
b: Everyone agreed that animals had to drink on the Sabbath; the debate was about how. The Damascus Document, a rule book linked with the Qumran community, limits how far an animal may be led to pasture on the Sabbath and forbids lifting it out of a pit (Damascus Document 11:5–6, 13–14). Rabbinic law allowed leading animals to water within limits. Jesus argues from a practice everyone accepted. The "manger" (phatnē) is the same word as the feeding trough where the baby Jesus was laid (2:7).

a: a daughter of Abraham
p: A rare title. In 4 Maccabees the martyred mother of seven sons is called a daughter of Abraham.
b: The phrase appears nowhere else in the New Testament. In 4 Maccabees 15:28 the mother who watched her seven sons die for the Law is praised as a daughter of Abraham in her courage. Jesus gives the title to a bent woman no one honored. She belongs to God's covenant people as fully as any son. Luke will call Zacchaeus "a son of Abraham" too (19:9). Abraham's children are the theme of John's preaching (3:8) and of the feast in 13:28.

a: Didn't she have to be untied
p: "Had to" is Luke's word dei, "it is necessary," used for what God's plan requires.
b: The synagogue leader said work "must" (dei) be done on six days (13:14). Jesus answers with the same word: she "had to" be untied on the Sabbath. In Luke dei often marks divine necessity: the boy Jesus "must" be in his Father's house (2:49), the Son of Man "must" suffer (9:22), Jesus "must" travel on to Jerusalem (13:33). The Sabbath is not merely a day when healing is allowed. It is the day when God's release most fittingly happens.

a: everyone who opposed him was put to shame
p: The wording recalls the Greek of Isaiah 45:16 and the "glorious things" God did for Israel in Exodus.
b: Commentators note that Luke's phrase follows the Septuagint of Isaiah 45:16, where all who oppose God are put to shame, and that "glorious things" (endoxa) is the Septuagint's word for God's wonders in Exodus 34:10. The crowd's joy at what God is doing contrasts with the leaders' embarrassment, a pattern Luke repeats (5:26; 7:16; 18:43; 19:37).

a: his own garden
t: A mustard seed in a garden
p: Matthew says field, Mark ground, Luke garden. Mustard spreads like a weed wherever it is sown.
b: Luke's "garden" (kēpos) suggests a Greek or Roman kitchen garden. Pliny the Elder notes (Natural History 19.170) that mustard, once sown, is hard to get rid of because it spreads so readily. Some scholars, such as John Dominic Crossan and Amy-Jill Levine in different ways, think the hearers would have found it a surprising picture for God's kingdom: not a noble cedar but a spreading, unstoppable plant.

a: It grew and turned into a tree
p: Birds nesting in a great tree stand in the prophets for the nations sheltering under a kingdom.
b: Mustard is an annual plant that can grow to the height of a man or more, but it is not really a tree. Calling it a tree points to the great trees of Ezekiel and Daniel, where birds of the sky nest in the branches as the nations under a great empire (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12, 21; compare Psalm 104:12). Luke's form is shorter than Mark's and Matthew's (Mark 4:30–32; Matthew 13:31–32), with no mention of the smallest seed. Placed after the healing of the bent woman, it suggests that small acts of release are the kingdom's beginning.
r: Ezekiel 17:23; Ezekiel 31:6; Daniel 4:12; Daniel 4:21; Psalm 104:12; Mark 4:30–32; Matthew 13:31–32

a: three measures of flour
p: Three measures was a huge amount of flour, enough bread for a large feast.
b: A saton (Hebrew se'ah) was a dry measure; estimates of its size vary, but three of them is commonly reckoned at about a bushel of flour, enough to bake bread for more than a hundred people. Sarah used the same amount when three visitors came to Abraham (Genesis 18:6). The woman "hid" the yeast: an odd verb for kneading, which underlines that the kingdom works unseen. Yeast is usually a sign of corruption (12:1), so its use here for the kingdom is surprising. See the note on Matthew 13:33.

a: pressing on with his journey to Jerusalem
p: Luke reminds the reader that the whole central section is a journey to Jerusalem.
b: At 9:51 Jesus "set his face" to go to Jerusalem. Luke's long central section (9:51–19:44) is framed as that journey, though it gives little geography. Luke repeats the reminder here and at 17:11; 18:31; 19:11, 28. The journey gives the teaching its weight: everything is said on the way to the city where Jesus will die (13:33).

a: are those being saved few in number?
t: Will only a few be saved?
p: A question Jewish teachers debated. 4 Ezra says the world to come is for few.
b: Jewish writers gave different answers. The Mishnah declares that "all Israel has a share in the world to come," with some exceptions (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). 4 Ezra, written after the temple's fall in AD 70, says the Most High made this age for many but the age to come for few (4 Ezra 8:1–3). Jesus does not give a number. He turns a speculative question into a personal command: make sure you yourself go in.

a: Fight your way in through the narrow door
p: Agōnizesthe is the word for athletes in a contest. Luke's door is the door of a house, not a city gate.
b: Agōnizomai, from which English gets "agony," describes a wrestler or runner straining to win (1 Corinthians 9:25; 1 Timothy 6:12). Matthew speaks of a narrow gate and a cramped road (Matthew 7:13–14). Luke's narrow door leads into a house, and the next verse shows why: the master of the house will lock it, and a banquet is going on inside (13:28–29). Many "will not have the strength": not because the door is hard to find, but because they come too late.

a: the master of the house gets up and locks the door
p: A picture close to the ten young women shut out of the wedding feast in Matthew 25.
b: In Matthew 25:10–12 the young women who were not ready arrive late, find the door shut, and call "Lord, Lord, open up for us!" only to hear that the groom does not know them. Luke's picture is similar but set at the master's own house. "I don't know where you are from" means "you are not of my household." A host knew his invited guests; latecomers who claim acquaintance are strangers.

a: We ate and drank in front of you
p: Jesus' own neighbors could claim they had shared meals with him and heard him teach in their streets.
b: The people outside appeal to acquaintance: Jesus ate and drank in their presence and taught in their town squares. First of all this addresses Jesus' own generation in Galilee and Judea, who saw and heard him. Christian readers have heard a warning to themselves as well: sharing the Lord's table and hearing his teaching do not take the place of following him (compare 1 Corinthians 10:1–12; 11:27–29). Matthew's form speaks of prophesying and miracles done in his name (Matthew 7:22).

a: Leave me, all you workers of wrong!
p: The judge's words come from Psalm 6:8, a sufferer's cry against his enemies.
b: The words follow the Greek of Psalm 6:8: "Leave me, every one of you who does wrong!" (Psalm 6:8). In the psalm a sick and persecuted man, sure that God has heard him, sends his enemies away. Matthew uses the same verse (Matthew 7:23). Luke's "workers of wrong" (ergatai adikias) differs from Matthew's "you who practice lawlessness." Both apply a psalm of David to the final judgment, where Jesus speaks God's verdict.

a: There people will weep and grind their teeth
p: Matthew's refrain for final loss. Luke uses it only here.
b: Matthew has this phrase six times (Matthew 8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30); Luke has it once. Grinding the teeth is a sign of anger and frustration as much as pain (Psalm 112:10; Acts 7:54). The pain here is seeing others at the feast: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, all the prophets, and people from every direction, while those who thought they belonged are outside.

a: from the sunrise and the sunset, from the north and the south
p: The prophets promised God would gather his people from every direction. Here they come to a feast.
b: Isaiah promised: "From the sunrise I will bring your offspring, and from the sunset I will gather you" (Isaiah 43:5), and "Look, these will come from far away" (Isaiah 49:12; compare Psalm 107:3). The feast in God's kingdom recalls Isaiah 25:6, where God spreads "a feast for all the peoples." Who are the people coming? Most read them as Gentiles, which fits Luke-Acts (Acts 10; 28:28). Some read them as scattered Jews returning, as in the prophets. Luke's own hearers would have seen both.
r: Isaiah 43:5–6; Isaiah 49:12; Psalm 107:3; Isaiah 25:6; Matthew 8:11; 14:15–24; Acts 28:28

a: some now last will be first
p: The reversal saying is in Mark and Matthew too. Luke's "some" softens it: not all the first will be last.
b: Mark and Matthew say "many of the first will be last" (Mark 10:31; Matthew 19:30) or "the last first, and the first last" (Matthew 20:16). Luke says "there are last who will be first, and there are first who will be last." It is a warning, not a rule that every insider is lost. Reversal is one of Luke's great themes: the mighty pulled down and the lowly lifted up (1:52), the poor blessed and the rich warned (6:20–26), the rich man and Lazarus (16:19–31).

a: some Pharisees came up to him
p: Did these Pharisees warn Jesus to save him, or to drive him out? Luke does not say.
b: Some interpreters suspect a trick: the Pharisees want Jesus out of Galilee, perhaps in league with Herod. Others take the warning at face value: some Pharisees, like Gamaliel in Acts 5:34–39, were fair-minded and did not want a prophet killed. Luke's portrait of Pharisees is mixed, and nothing in the text says they were lying. Jesus' reply does not rebuke them. Amy-Jill Levine and others warn readers against assuming that every Pharisee in the Gospels is a villain.

a: Herod wants to kill you
p: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea for Rome. He had already beheaded John the Baptist.
b: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC to AD 39. He had imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist (3:19–20; 9:9), and was curious about Jesus (9:7–9). Luke alone reports that he later questioned Jesus in Jerusalem (23:6–12). Antipas built Tiberias as his capital; Jesus is never said to have entered it or Sepphoris.

a: this fox
p: A fox was cunning, destructive and small: not a lion. The insult may carry all three.
b: In Greek and Jewish usage the fox was a sly animal. It was also a petty one: the Mishnah's saying "be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes" (Mishnah Avot 4:15) sets foxes below lions. Nehemiah's enemy mocked that "If a fox went up on it, he would breach their wall of stones" (Nehemiah 4:3). The Song of Songs speaks of foxes that ruin vineyards (Song of Songs 2:15). Jesus calls Antipas a crafty, destructive little ruler who cannot change God's timetable.

a: on the third day I am brought to completion
p: The verb teleioumai means "I reach my goal" or "I am made perfect." It points to Jesus' death and what follows.
b: "Today and tomorrow" is a Semitic way of saying "for a short while," and "the third day" the end of that time. Readers of Luke also hear the third day of the resurrection (9:22; 24:7, 46). Teleioumai is passive: "I am completed, perfected." Hebrews uses the same verb for Jesus made perfect through suffering (Hebrews 2:10; 5:9). Jesus' work will not be ended by Herod's threat but finished by God's plan in Jerusalem (compare John 19:30).

a: It won't do for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem
p: Bitter irony: Jerusalem is the city where prophets are killed. Not every prophet died there.
b: The saying is not a law: many prophets died elsewhere, and John the Baptist was executed at Herod's fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea (Josephus, Antiquities 18.119). It is an ironic proverb. Jerusalem's record, from Zechariah in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:21) to Uriah killed by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20–23), makes it the fitting place for the last prophet's death. The Lives of the Prophets tells of several prophets killed in or near Jerusalem.

a: the way a bird gathers her brood under her wings
p: The Bible pictures God sheltering his people under his wings. Jesus speaks of himself in that role.
b: "Beneath his wings you can take shelter" (Psalm 91:4); "Hide me in the shade of your wings" (Psalm 17:8); Ruth came "under whose wings you have come for refuge" (Ruth 2:12). Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God as an eagle spreading its wings over its young. In this lament Jesus takes up the image for himself, speaking as God or as God's Wisdom longing over the city. "How many times" hints at more visits to Jerusalem than Luke records, as John's Gospel describes.
r: Psalm 91:4; Psalm 17:8; Psalm 36:7; Ruth 2:12; Deuteronomy 32:11; Isaiah 31:5; Matthew 23:37

a: your house is abandoned to you
t: A house left on its own
p: Jeremiah warned that God would abandon his house. In Luke the lament comes before the entry into Jerusalem.
b: "Your house" can mean the temple, the city or the ruling families. Jeremiah's words lie behind it: God says he has left his house and abandoned his inheritance (Jeremiah 12:7), and that the king's house will become a ruin (Jeremiah 22:5). Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the temple (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:22–23). Matthew places these words after Jesus has entered Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37–39). Luke places them on the road, so they look ahead to 19:41–44 and the city's fall in AD 70.

a: you will never see me
p: Fulfilled at the triumphal entry, or a hope for Israel's future welcome of the Messiah?
b: The words quote Psalm 118:26, the pilgrims' greeting at the temple: "Blessed is the one who comes in the LORD's name!" (Psalm 118:26). In Luke the crowd of disciples will cry nearly these words, adding "the King," as Jesus rides into Jerusalem (19:38), so some read the saying as fulfilled there. Others note that it is the disciples, not the city, who say them, and read a promise that Jerusalem will one day welcome the Messiah at his return (Acts 3:19–21; Romans 11:25–26). Others hear a sentence of judgment: they will see him only when it is too late. The churches' views of Israel's future are compared at Isaiah 59:20. Some editions read simply "until you say"; see the variant.
